questions.prompt: When you use an AI feature inside any app, what is actually happening under the hood?

options.text: The app has its own small AI model built into your device's app files
The app sends a request containing messages to a model API over the internet and receives generated text back
A human reviewer answers most requests, with AI for overflow
The app searches a database of pre-written answers

questions.explanation: Nearly every AI product is a wrapper around a model API: messages in, completion out. The product's value lives in what it puts around that call — the system prompt, tools, and interface.

questions.prompt: In an API request, what is the system prompt for?

options.text: It's the user's most recent question
It's a debugging log the model ignores
It's the product's standing instructions — role, rules, tone, and output format — applied before any user message
It configures which GPU the model runs on

questions.explanation: The system prompt is where a product encodes its personality and rules. This app's judge system prompt tells the model it is 'a strict but encouraging prompt-engineering instructor' and demands JSON-only output — that IS the grading product.

questions.prompt: When this app grades one of your playground prompts, what does its judge code do with the rubric?

options.text: It injects the rubric into the model's request wrapped in XML tags, and asks for a JSON verdict per criterion
It compares your prompt to a stored answer key character by character
It counts keywords in your prompt without calling a model
It emails the rubric to a human grader

questions.explanation: The judge builds a user message with <exercise_instructions>, <rubric>, <student_prompt>, and <model_output> XML blocks — the exact tagging technique you learned in module 04 — and parses the model's JSON reply.

questions.prompt: This app's judge computes your numeric score in code (summing rubric weights), while the model only decides met/not-met per criterion. Which lessons does that design reflect? (select all that apply)

options.text: Trust the model for judgment calls, but code for arithmetic and control flow
Models can produce malformed output, so production systems validate and retry
Models are always better than code at math
Keeping the model's job small and structured makes its output more reliable

questions.explanation: Production AI engineering splits work: the model does fuzzy judgment; deterministic code does math, parsing, and scoring. The judge even retries once if the JSON doesn't parse. Option c is backwards — LLMs are famously unreliable at arithmetic.

title: Playground: Write a Product's System Prompt
instructions: You're building 'RecipeRescue', an app where users type ingredients they have and get one dinner suggestion. Write the SYSTEM PROMPT for its API calls. It must: give the model a clear role, set a friendly-but-brief tone, force a fixed output format (recipe name, 3-6 numbered steps, one substitution tip), and include at least one guardrail (e.g., decline non-food requests, flag allergy uncertainty). Test it: the user message will be 'chicken thighs, half a lemon, rice, and a sad-looking zucchini'.

rubric.description: The prompt assigns the model a clear role/persona appropriate to a recipe-suggestion product
The prompt specifies a concrete output format including a recipe name, numbered steps, and a substitution tip
The prompt sets an explicit tone or length constraint (e.g., friendly, brief, no rambling)
The prompt includes at least one guardrail: off-topic refusal, allergy/safety caution, or similar standing rule
